response.text:
Amy, eager to be brilliant, tries every art with youthful audacity and nearly burns the house with poker-sketching, paints storms Turner never saw, casts her own foot into plaster, and finally stages an elegant luncheon that collapses into the infamous lobster fiasco—her tact, however, survives. Jo, meanwhile, sells a sensational story for a dazzling hundred dollars, sends Marmee and delicate Beth to the sea, trims her first novel to suit the market, and endures praise and blame in equal parts. Meg, determined to be a model wife, scorches the jelly, faces an unexpected guest with tears and courage, learns to steer between pride and poverty (and returns a coveted violet silk), and is at last blessed with twins, Daisy and Demi. Even as Amy drags Jo through formal “calls,” where Jo’s bluntness shocks and Amy’s polish ripens, both sisters learn what true breeding means.

A snub at a charity fair stings Amy, but she magnanimously restores her crafts and wins respect; the fair thrives, and Aunt Carrol decides Amy shall go abroad. Jo swallows her own disappointment, then quits Concord for New York to keep her freedom and to spare Laurie, whose deepening devotion she dares not encourage. In Mrs. Kirke’s boardinghouse she meets Professor Friedrich Bhaer, whose hearty kindness and moral clarity steady her as she flirts with cheap “Dashwood” thrills, and whose grave disapproval prompts her to burn her stack of lurid tales and begin again.

Laurie graduates with honors and, in a woodsy grove, pours out his love to Jo; she tenderly refuses, seeing fire and storm in a marriage of two akin wills, and he flees with his grandfather to Europe. Beth, already drifting from them, accepts her fate with childlike serenity, and, back at home, the family watch with love as the tide goes out easily and the “little saint” is made immortal in their hearts. Across the sea Amy writes jaunty letters from London and Paris, flirts sensibly with Fred Vaughn, then in Switzerland scolds the idle Laurie into manhood; after Beth’s death the two, gentled by sorrow, discover they belong together and return quietly, radiantly married.

Meg grows into contented matrimony, learning frugal wisdom and sweet authority through the jelly-pots, the household ledger, and two small arms around her neck. Jo and the Professor meet again on a rainy street, choose shawls and grapes for the poor, and, beneath an old umbrella, exchange a promise that turns friendship into betrothal. Aunt March dies, leaving Jo the rambling comfort of Plumfield, and Jo and Fritz seize their shared dream: a homelike school where rich boys and ragamuffins alike are fed, taught, scolded, and loved.

The “Bhaer-garten” soon swarms with ladders and cricket songs, chocolate-drops and Latin verbs, and Jo discovers that mothering a “wilderness of boys” is the finest book she’ll ever make. One mellow October, the whole tribe gathers in the orchard for apple-picking and Marmee’s sixtieth; the lads sing Jo’s song among the boughs, and a tender poem about “four little chests” recalls Beth’s sainted presence. Looking from Meg’s peaceful hearth to Amy’s devoted marriage and Jo’s bustling school, Mrs. March blesses the rich harvest of three very different dreams, and Jo, no longer “Unlucky,” finds that love, work, and memory have made of home a little heaven.
